item.title: FG moves to tackle illegal fishing, maritime threats in Gulf of Guinea
item.description: By Folarin Kehinde The Federal Government has moved to strengthen the fight against illegal fishing and maritime threats in the Gulf of Guinea through a proposed regional Marine and Blue Economy Policy aimed at improving security, attracting investment and deepening cooperation among member states. Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, said a common regional policy would enable countries to tackle shared maritime challenges and promote the sustainable use of marine resources. Oyetola spoke while presenting two draft policy documents to the Deputy Executive Secretary of the Gulf of Guinea Commission (GGC), Ambassador Obinna Agbugba, for consideration by the regional body. The minister in a press statement by his Special Adviser, Dr. Bolaji Akinola disclosed that the Commission had formally requested him to lead the development of a comprehensive regional Marine and Blue Economy Policy in a letter dated May 7, 2026. Following the request, he said he constituted a multi-stakeholder committee comprising technical departments of the Federal Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy and the Department of Planning, Research and Statistics to drive the process. The committee produced a draft Strategic Plan for the Development and Operationalisation of a Gulf of Guinea Commission Policy on Marine and Blue Economy (2026–2030), as well as a draft Policy Framework and Strategy Template. According to Oyetola, the documents outline strategic priorities, proposed interventions, performance indicators, implementation timelines, lead agencies and funding considerations. He said the proposed framework would strengthen collaboration among member states, promote investment and support coordinated action against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. The minister added that the drafts were developed in consideration of the 2025 Yaoundé Declaration and the work of the United Nations Task Force supporting the Commission’s 2026 Work Plan. To ensure effective coordination, Oyetola proposed the establishment of a Steering Committee to guide policy development and coordinate stakeholder engagement, recommending that the Federal Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy serve as its secretariat. He also called for inclusive consultations involving member states, relevant institutions and stakeholders to ensure regional ownership of the policy. Earlier, Agbugba commended Nigeria’s development of its first National Policy on Marine and Blue Economy, describing the initiative as an important foundation for the Commission’s regional policy ambition. Agbugba, who spoke on behalf of the Commission’s Executive Secretary, José Mba Abeso, expressed confidence in Oyetola’s leadership of the process. item.description: By Gift ChapiOdekina, Abuja The House of Representatives has begun moves to establish a regulatory framework for nutrition practice in Nigeria, with lawmakers and stakeholders meeting on Tuesday to consider a bill seeking to establish the Nutritionists Registration Council of Nigeria. The proposed legislation is aimed at strengthening professional standards, improving the quality of nutrition services and protecting Nigerians from harmful or misleading nutritional advice. Declaring the public hearing open, Speaker of the House, Tajudeen Abbas, said the establishment of a Standing Committee on Nutrition and Food Security reflected the importance of nutrition to public health, education, healthcare expenditure and national productivity. He urged stakeholders to contribute constructively to the process, stressing that the proposed law must address clearly identified needs and provide a workable framework for regulating the profession. “I urge all stakeholders to approach this hearing with candour, technical rigour and a shared commitment to national interest. item.title: Lekki shooting: Why didn’t you ask Buhari? Tinubu’s aide faults Atiku’s EndSARS question
item.description: President Bola Tinubu’s Special Assistant on Social Media, Dada Olusegun, has faulted former Vice President Atiku Abubakar for demanding accountability over the October 2020 Lekki Toll Gate shooting, asking why he did not raise the issue during his visits to former President Muhammadu Buhari. Olusegun accused Atiku of exploiting the sixth anniversary of the #EndSARS protests to advance his presidential ambition, arguing that the former vice president had opportunities to question Buhari, who was president when the shooting occurred. In a statement responding to Atiku’s call for answers, the presidential aide recalled that the former vice president visited Buhari in Daura, Katsina State, on June 22, 2024, and again at his retirement residence in Kaduna on April 11, 2025. “Those two opportunities presented you with chances to ask former President Buhari, who was President at the time of the Lekki Toll Gate protests, the questions you are now asking President Tinubu,” Olusegun said. He added that Atiku’s decision to raise the issue six years after the incident showed, in his view, that the former vice president was being politically insincere. “That it took you six years to ask these questions is a testament to your insincerity and desperation to become President,” he said. Atiku had, in a post on his X account on Tuesday, renewed calls for accountability over the shooting, which occurred during the #EndSARS protests against police brutality. “Six years after the Lekki shooting, Nigeria is still waiting for a clear answer to one devastating question: Who gave the order?” the former vice president asked. The wait for payouts is stretching longer than expected, and that pause is starting to feel uncomfortable. For many in Nigeria and beyond, what should be a celebration quickly turns into a tense waiting game. Across social media and gambling forums, players are sharing their frustrations, comparing notes, and wondering why the money isn’t showing up. The joy of betting is changing, as doubts creep in about what’s really happening behind those delayed withdrawals. From anticipation to unease: how winning feels different when payouts stall Instead of the usual thrill that comes right after a win, many players now feel an uneasy pause as they wait for their money to clear. The excitement of seeing a bet come through fades as the hours drag on and the payout still hasn’t landed. Some people find themselves glued to their transaction history, refreshing pages and double-checking balances, hoping each update finally brings good news. What should be a quick reward often turns into a long, anxious watch—and that waiting period can turn even the happiest moments sour. Players start to talk about their experiences in detail, comparing cash-out times not just with friends but also through online communities. Some gamblers quietly step back from sites that make them wait, or they start spreading their bets across different platforms just in case. Others admit they feel cheated, even if the money eventually shows up. There’s a sense that the system is no longer fully on the player’s side. Industry numbers tell a reassuring story: nearly all withdrawals are processed right away. But those rare slowdowns dominate the conversation, making people wonder if their next payout might be the exception. Suspicion doesn’t need proof—it only needs a pause. Behavioral shifts: how bettors respond to new uncertainties This growing anxiety around delayed withdrawals is quietly changing the way people gamble online. Instead of focusing on the thrill of picking winners, many now think about how quickly they can get their money out—sometimes even before placing a bet. Some players react by cashing out more often and in smaller amounts, hoping to avoid the stress of a big sum getting stuck. Others split their bets across different sites, or only use platforms that friends say pay out without issues. For a few, all it takes is a single bad experience for them to start keeping detailed records of every transaction, or to simply stop using a site altogether. It’s not just about moving money faster; these habits reflect a deeper shift in priorities. Speed and trust now matter more than flashy bonuses or boosted odds. Online, conversations have changed as well. People swap stories about reliable sites and share tips for avoiding delays, instead of just celebrating wins or trading betting advice. If you want a sense of how these changes are playing out, Player reactions to delays offers a window into the new mindset. Even small inconveniences are enough to send bettors looking elsewhere, reshaping the community and raising the bar for what counts as a good betting experience. Behind the delays: What the data and research reveal The shift in player behavior isn’t happening in a vacuum. Underneath every frustrated conversation, there’s a story in the numbers that shows just how rare—yet disruptive—cash-out delays really are. Industry data paints a reassuring picture at first glance. The vast majority of withdrawals actually happen instantly, with over 96 percent processed right away and almost all the rest cleared within a day. Only a tiny fraction ever take longer. Still, those rare drawn-out waits are what people remember most, echoing across forums and turning one person’s bad experience into a cautionary tale for everyone else. Regulators like the UK Gambling Commission keep a close watch on these trends, tracking how quickly sites move money from account to account. They’re not ignoring the outliers, either. Even the smallest percentage of slow payouts is enough to prompt new questions about how well the system is working, and whether companies are doing everything they can to keep trust intact. Research tries to answer some of these worries with practical solutions. For example, a recent study on personalized messages found that simple reminders can nudge players to withdraw their winnings more promptly, which might help avoid those moments when hesitation or confusion leads to bigger losses. But the story doesn’t end at speed. Reports from financial watchdogs highlight that extra hurdles—like cash advance fees when using credit cards—add another layer of frustration for bettors already anxious about delays. Sometimes the fee itself is enough to make a quick withdrawal feel less like a win and more like a setback. Every new complication, whether it’s a processing lag or a hidden charge, feeds the larger debate about fairness and transparency in online gambling. Each one changes how players feel, how they act, and how they talk about the games they once trusted without a second thought. What happens next: trust, regulation, and the future of online betting The more these delays and fees become everyday topics, the more players demand change. Calls for clearer rules and faster payment standards are growing louder, both among bettors and regulators. Some industry experts point out that even rare issues can damage trust for a long time. Open communication and quick payouts may be the only way to hold onto loyal players in this shifting environment. Regulators are looking at new policies, while players want gambling sites and banks to take more responsibility. The CFPB report on credit card fees adds to the urgency, showing how extra costs can sour the whole experience. If something doesn’t change soon, the thrill of betting online might give way to constant worry, and more people could hold back before placing their next wager. item.title: My mission is to demonstrate power; I don’t collect tithes – Odumeje
item.description: General Overseer of Mountain of Holy Ghost Intervention and Deliverance Ministry, Prophet Chukwuemeka Ohanaemere, popularly known as Odumeje, has said his ministry does not collect tithes, insisting that his primary mission is to demonstrate spiritual power. The cleric disclosed this during an appearance on the Honest Bunch Podcast, in an episode uploaded to YouTube on Monday. Odumeje criticised churches that frequently preach about tithing, accusing some of prioritising money collection over demonstrating spiritual power and performing miracles. He said, “Those people that collect tithes and teach tithes every day when you come to church, they will be interested in making sure that they clear your pockets. And there is no practical evidence and miracles that you will see. The only thing is stories. That is not the kind of church I run.” Explaining his ministry’s focus, he added, “My mission on earth is demonstration of power. All the teaching of tithe and teaching of giving, I am not in that area.” However, Odumeje clarified that he did not consider tithing wrong, maintaining that the decision to pay should be left to individuals and their relationship with God. “I don’t collect tithes. Nobody pays me tithes. I am not saying that tithe is bad. It’s a decision between you and God if you want to pay tithe. Tithe is real. But it is something that you must decide. Not something that somebody will be brainwashing you, forcing you,” he said. The cleric also condemned teachings suggesting that Christians would be denied access to heaven if they failed to pay tithes. item.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri, Abuja The Federal High Court in Abuja, on Tuesday, declined to declare vacant the seat of the House of Representatives member for Igabi Federal Constituency of Kaduna State, Hussaini Jallo, following his alleged defection to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). The court, in a judgment delivered by Justice James Omotosho, held that the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) failed to provide any credible evidence to prove Jallo’s defection. It held that although the PDP has the legal right to institute the action as a necessary party, it was unable to establish that the lawmaker took its votes to the APC. According to the court, a political party which sponsored a candidate who has allegedly defected is fully clothed with the requisite locus standi to bring a court action to compel the Speaker of the House of Representatives to declare the defecting member’s seat vacant. Justice Omotosho held that by virtue of the provisions of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, once an elected legislator in the National Assembly defects to another party, he automatically loses his seat. “The proviso to this section, however, provides for an exception where such defection was on the grounds of division within the party,” he added. He held that, having observed the exhibits tendered by the PDP, one of which was a newspaper publication alleging the defection, there was no concrete evidence of the lawmaker’s membership of the APC. item.title: Policymakers must prioritise durable skills for future workplaces – HP Futures 2026 report
item.description: By Elizabeth Osayande A new global report, HP Futures 2026, has urged policymakers in Nigeria and worldwide to prioritise durable skills such as creativity, critical thinking, communication and collaboration that will be essential in workplaces of the future. The report, led by HP, the Global Learning Council, and the Education Leaders Forum, convened 58 education, policymaking and future of work leaders globally to examine how education systems can equip young people for the future of work. item.title: World Cup: FIFA suspends Egypt coach, forward for criticising referee after Argentina defeat
item.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye FIFA has suspended Egypt coach Hossam Hassan for three matches and forward Mostafa Zico for five games following their criticism of the referee after the country’s 3-2 defeat by Argentina at the World Cup. According to Reuters, the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) announced the sanctions on Monday, adding that Egypt’s national team director, Ibrahim Hassan, the twin brother of Hossam, had also received a three-match suspension. Hossam was sanctioned for blaming refereeing errors for Egypt’s elimination from the tournament in the last 16, while Zico was punished for insulting the referee during a post-match interview. The EFA confirmed the disciplinary decisions in a statement, saying it had requested the detailed grounds for the sanctions from FIFA’s Disciplinary Committee to assess its legal options and determine whether to appeal. The controversy followed a disputed sequence of decisions during Egypt’s defeat to Argentina, with Zico having a goal disallowed for a foul in the build-up before Egypt’s players appealed for a penalty late in the match when the score was 2-2. However, FIFA refereeing chief Pierluigi Collina defended the officiating, warning that allegations against referees could expose them and their families to threats. The suspensions could affect Egypt’s preparations for their upcoming Africa Cup of Nations qualifying matches against Malawi in November, with Hossam and Ibrahim Hassan potentially missing those fixtures and the opening match of the March international window. Zico’s five-match suspension could keep him out of action for Egypt until June. He said the figures demonstrated the growing importance of Customs to Nigeria’s public finances and the need to close revenue leakages without placing unnecessary burdens on legitimate businesses. He added that, under the new tax laws, 90 per cent of value-added tax collected on imports was allocated to states and local governments. “When a smuggler evades duty, he does not cheat an abstraction called government. He cheats a pupil, a nurse and a farmer,” he said. Adeniyi traced the Service’s revenue growth from N3.2 trillion in 2023 to N6.105 trillion in 2024 and N7.28 trillion in 2025, attributing the improvement to stronger compliance, improved valuation, digital systems and enforcement. He said the Service was determined to meet its 2026 target by reducing revenue leakages rather than obstructing legitimate trade. “We will pursue the target through compliance, data and facilitation, not through harassment at the ports, because a target met by choking trade would be a false victory,” he said. The Customs chief also cited the need to address illicit financial flows and trade misinvoicing, through which importers and exporters manipulate the declared value or description of goods to evade taxes, duties and other financial obligations. He said such practices weakened the country’s revenue base and undermined the integrity of its trade system. Adeniyi noted that Africa’s tax-to-GDP ratio stood at about 16.1 per cent, compared with approximately 33.9 per cent for countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, highlighting the continent’s broader challenge of mobilising domestic revenue. He said Customs had a critical role to play in closing the gap by improving the accuracy of declarations, strengthening risk assessment and ensuring that eligible transactions were properly assessed. Adeniyi said the Service was deploying digital platforms and data analytics to improve the assessment of imports, detect suspicious declarations and reduce delays at the ports. He disclosed that the B’Odogwu cargo-processing platform handled approximately 16,000 entries and generated N120 billion in revenue in its first three months at the Port and Terminal Multi-Services Limited Command. He said the National Single Window, which went live on March 27, 2026, was intended to connect trade-related government processes and reduce duplication in documentation. “A study conducted at Tin Can Island Port showed that cargo release took almost five days on average, with more than 90 per cent of the time spent waiting.“ The Service, he said, was working towards reducing cargo clearance to 24 hours in the long term, with an interim target of two days and a plan to rely on scanning rather than physical examination for 99 per cent of cargo. He added that 51 companies certified under the Authorised Economic Operator programme had reduced their clearance time from 168 hours to 41 hours, while demurrage costs fell by approximately 90 per cent. According to him, the improvements showed that revenue collection and trade facilitation could reinforce each other when procedures were efficient and compliance was properly managed. Adeniyi said revenue protection could not be separated from national security, citing the interception of 399 pump-action rifles and hundreds of firearm components concealed in a container discharged from the vessel MV Velika at Tin Can Island Port in July 2026. The weapons were handed over to the National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons, while the case remained before the Federal High Court. He also recalled the seizure of 844 rifles and 112,500 rounds of ammunition at Onne, Rivers State, in June 2024, as well as the handover of 1,599 firearms seized between 2018 and 2024 to the national centre in February 2025. The Customs chief said the Service had also intercepted 25 containers of fake and unregistered medicines worth approximately N9.2 billion in July 2025. On wildlife trafficking, he cited the seizure of 3.76 tonnes of pangolin scales in Lagos in April 2025, representing at least 1,900 animals, and said enforcement operations since 2021 had led to seizures of more than 25 tonnes of pangolin scales and over one tonne of ivory, with 12 convictions secured. He also highlighted fuel smuggling, drug trafficking and the illegal movement of food commodities as activities that threatened public safety, economic stability and government revenue. On border management, Adeniyi argued that intelligence-led enforcement and cooperation with neighbouring countries were more sustainable than blanket border closures. He said Nigeria’s land-border closure between August 2019 and December 2020 curtailed some smuggling activities but did not eliminate the networks behind the illegal trade. “The lesson is that a nation is protected by intelligent control of its border, not by sealing it. Closure is a blunt instrument, while intelligence, data and joint patrols with our neighbours are sharper ones,” he said. He called for closer cooperation with border communities and neighbouring countries, while urging traders to use legitimate channels under regional trade arrangements such as the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme. Adeniyi also said Nigeria’s participation in the African Continental Free Trade Area depended on effective customs administration to verify the origin of goods and ensure that preferential trade arrangements were properly implemented. Imports from other African countries accounted for approximately four per cent of Nigeria’s total imports in 2025, he said, suggesting significant room for expanding intra-African trade. The Comptroller-General proposed a structured partnership with the University of Ibadan’s Centre of Excellence in Security Management to improve research on border economies, trade compliance and illicit financial flows. item.title: Meet Nigeria’s youngest female SAN, Olamide Ehinfun-Adekunle
item.description: Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun-Adekunle has made history as Nigeria’s youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), attaining the prestigious legal rank at the age of 40. She was among 68 legal practitioners sworn in as Senior Advocates of Nigeria by the Chief Justice of Nigeria, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, on October 12, 2026, during the opening of the 2026/2027 legal year. Four women were among the newly elevated practitioners. Born on June 25, 1986, in Kaduna State, Ehinfun-Adekunle hails from Ijero-Ekiti in Ekiti State. Her journey into the legal profession began with her studies at Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, where she obtained her Bachelor of Laws degree between 2003 and 2009. She proceeded to the Nigerian Law School, where she studied from 2009 to 2010, before earning a Master of Laws degree in International Trade Law from the University of Leeds, United Kingdom, between 2011 and 2012. She is also a member of the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators in the UK. Before joining Afe Babalola & Co. in September 2013, Ehinfun-Adekunle worked at D. D. Dodo & Co. and the Nuhu Ribadu Campaign Organisation. She subsequently became a partner at Afe Babalola & Co., where her areas of practice include complex litigation, commercial dispute resolution, oil and gas, arbitration, election petitions, transactional law and regulatory compliance. Her professional experience has also included appearances before the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Nigeria. The Legal Practitioners’ Privileges Committee approved her elevation to the rank of SAN on July 23, 2026, before she was formally sworn in alongside 67 other legal practitioners in October. Ehinfun-Adekunle’s interest in law reportedly developed during her childhood. Her parents described her as talkative, a trait also reflected in her primary school reports. Stories told by her father about politics in the old Western Region and the legal career of Chief Rotimi Williams, popularly known as “Timi the Law”, helped shape her interest in the profession. Several prominent figures have influenced her career, including Aare Afe Babalola, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, Kehinde Ogunwumiju and Pastor R. A. Ogunwole. Beyond her legal practice, Ehinfun-Adekunle has spoken about the challenges confronting Nigeria’s justice system, particularly delays in the administration of justice and the financial burden prolonged litigation places on individuals and businesses. item.title: Imo Kidnap: Five Suspects Plead Not Guilty To Abducting Corps Members, Four Others
item.description: Five suspects accused of kidnapping 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members and four other persons in Imo State have pleaded not guilty to the charges against them following their arraignment before the Justice Oputa State High Court in Owerri. The defendants face a three-count charge bordering on conspiracy, hostage-taking and unlawful possession of firearms. Three of the suspects — 25-year-old Usman Aliyu, also known as Chonge; 21-year-old Babangida Aliyu; and 23-year-old Mohammed Ali, alias Smallie Pepper — are accused of abducting the prospective corps members on October 1, 2026, Nigeria’s Independence Day. According to the charge sheet, the trio allegedly demanded and collected ₦48 million and an undisclosed amount in US dollars for the release of the victims. They were also accused of unlawfully possessing three AK-47 rifles, four magazines, a pistol and 81 rounds of live ammunition. The prosecuting counsel said the charge of conspiracy to commit hostage-taking is punishable under Section 6 of the Imo State Prohibition of Hostage Taking and Related Offences Law No. 4 of 2009. The other two defendants, 27-year-old Aminu Haliru and 20-year-old Tange Ibrahim, also known as Jijji, are accused of abducting four persons around Owerri and Mgbidi on October 4, four days after the first abduction. The prosecution alleged that Haliru, Ibrahim and other suspects still at large collected ₦8 million for the release of the four victims. They also face allegations of unlawfully possessing an AK-47 rifle and a pump-action gun. The presiding judge, Justice Emeka Orafu, adjourned the trial until Thursday, October 22, 2026. The victims were abducted by gunmen near Umunoha in Mbaitoli Local Government Area on October 1, 2026, while travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to their assigned NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states. The abduction sparked a security operation to locate the victims and apprehend those responsible. On October 7, the 20 prospective corps members and the civilian were rescued from the Amakohia-Ubi forest in Owerri West Local Government Area. They subsequently received medical attention at the DSS hospital in Owerri. The DSS later arrested five suspects in intelligence-led operations conducted between October 10 and 14 in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, and Aba, Abia State. The operations involved a joint security team led by the DSS, working with the military, police and other security operatives. Three other suspects reportedly escaped with gunshot wounds, prompting a manhunt for them and other fleeing members of the suspected kidnapping syndicate. The arraignment marks a further step in the investigation into the abduction, as the prosecution of the five arrested suspects gets underway. item.title: Eniola Badmus apologises to Laide Bakare, calls for end to feud
item.description: Nollywood actress Eniola Badmus has apologised to her colleague, Laide Bakare, following the backlash over her reaction to Bakare’s name during a recent podcast appearance, expressing a desire to put their differences behind them. Badmus tendered the apology in a statement shared on Instagram on Tuesday, days after a clip from her appearance on Isbae U’s Curiosity Made Me Ask podcast went viral on social media. During the interview, the host mentioned Bakare as one of his favourite actresses, prompting Badmus to hiss and change her facial expression. The moment attracted reactions online and revived discussions about the strained relationship between the two actresses. Reflecting on her reaction via her Instagram page, Badmus admitted that it could have been perceived as dismissive and expressed regret over how it came across. “On reflection, I realise my reaction when Laide Bakare’s name was mentioned during my recent interview could have come across as dismissive, and for that, I sincerely apologise,” she wrote. Addressing Bakare directly, the actress added, “Laide, whatever our differences, I choose peace and I genuinely wish you well.” Badmus said maturity involves learning from past experiences and choosing to move forward rather than holding on to disagreements. “We’re all growing, learning and becoming better versions of ourselves. Sometimes maturity is simply knowing when to let go and move forward,” she stated. She concluded her message with a plea for peace, writing, “Joo maa binu. No negativity. No grudges. Let love lead and peace reigns.” The apology comes amid a history of public disagreements between the actresses, whose relationship has been marked by exchanges on social media and confrontations at public events. In March 2024, Badmus appeared to mock Bakare’s outfit at the latter’s book launch. Bakare had attended the event in a white outfit with an orange cape, which generated mixed reactions online. Badmus subsequently took to Instagram and wrote, “Ewo ninu yin lo wo Aso Pastor Ajidara. Abeg who??” The remark was widely interpreted as a dig at Bakare’s outfit. Bakare expressed disappointment over the incident, questioning why a colleague she regarded as a childhood friend from their University of Ibadan days would publicly criticise her instead of celebrating her achievement. item.title: #EndSARS: No Nigerian should be punished for demanding good governance – Obi
item.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has said no Nigerian should be punished for demanding good governance, as he marked six years since the October 20, 2020, incident at the Lekki Toll Gate. “Nigeria must become a nation where no citizen is punished for demanding good governance and a better future,” Obi said in a statement posted on X on Tuesday. Obi described the anniversary as a reminder of the price Nigerian youths paid in their demand for a better country. “Today, October 20, 2026, marks the sixth anniversary of the Lekki Toll Gate shootings, a painful reminder of the price Nigerian youths paid in their demand for a better country.” He recalled the events of October 20, 2020, saying peaceful protesters faced gunfire and that lives were lost, and many people were injured, leaving questions about justice, accountability and the value placed on human life. “On that fateful night, peaceful #EndSARS protesters were met with gunfire. Lives were lost, many were injured, and the nation was left with questions about justice, accountability, and the sanctity of human life.” Calling on Nigerians to remember the victims and resist treating injustice as normal, Obi said: “We must never forget. We must never normalise injustice.” He also noted that the anniversary reinforced his belief in a “New Nigeria,” describing it as a country where citizens are protected, young people are heard, and those in government exercise power responsibly and respect human rights. “As we remember the victims, I reaffirm my belief that a New Nigeria is possible—a country where citizens are protected, not brutalised; where young people are heard, not silenced; and where government power is exercised with responsibility and respect for human rights.” Obi added that the victims’ sacrifice should strengthen efforts to ensure the incident is not repeated while praying for those who died. “May the souls of the departed continue to rest in peace. May their sacrifice strengthen our resolve to build a Nigeria where this tragedy will never be repeated.” He ended the statement by reiterating his vision of a country where every life matters. The Lagos State Judicial Panel of Inquiry’s 2021 report found that Nigerian Army officers shot, injured and killed unarmed protesters at the Lekki Toll Gate, and said the manner of assault and killing could be described as a massacre in context. Vanguard reported that the panel identified at least 48 protesters who were shot, injured or assaulted. item.title: #EndSARS Anniversary: Police Fire Tear Gas To Disperse Gathering At Lekki Toll Gate
item.description: Tension flared at the Lekki Toll Gate as police fired tear gas to disperse activists and concerned Nigerians who gathered to commemorate the sixth anniversary of the #EndSARS protests. The gathering was organised to honour those who lost their lives and remember the demonstrations against police brutality. The protesters were forced to flee as tear gas filled the area, disrupting the planned commemoration. Among those who gathered at the toll gate were the Lagos State governorship candidates of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Funso Doherty, and the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour. ﻿ Despite the disruption, the activists vowed to continue the struggle for justice and police reforms that inspired the #EndSARS protests, while keeping alive the memory of those who died. Tension has since subsided, and the area is now clear. Police operatives use teargas to disperse a gathering at the Lekki Toll Gate during the sixth anniversary of the #EndSARS protests. Six years after the protests, the incident has renewed concerns about citizens’ right to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression. Tuesday’s incident comes six years after the protests that began in October 2020, as young Nigerians demanded an end to police brutality, particularly abuses associated with the now-disbanded Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS). Woman defies police teargas, honours #EndSARS victims on the sixth memorial at Lekki Tollgate The demonstrations spread across the country, with the Lekki Toll Gate becoming a focal point of the movement. On October 20, 2020, soldiers opened fire on protesters at the toll gate, an incident that remains a source of controversy over casualties and accountability. The Lagos State Judicial Panel of Inquiry, which investigated the incident, found that protesters were shot at, injured and killed. The state government later rejected key parts of the panel’s findings, including aspects of its conclusions on casualties. The anniversary has also been marked by clashes between security operatives and people who gathered at the toll gate in subsequent years. In October 2021, police fired tear gas during a memorial procession organised by youths and celebrities to honour victims of police brutality. The then Lagos Commissioner of Police, Hakeem Odumosu, said the officers were dispersing people he described as “miscreants”, rather than participants in the procession. In 2024, police again fired tear gas to disperse protesters marking the fourth anniversary. The protesters had called for the full implementation of recommendations made by judicial panels established after the 2020 demonstrations. The police said they acted after the protesters refused to disperse. The #EndSARS movement led to the disbandment of SARS in October 2020, but demands for accountability, compensation for victims and broader police reforms have continued.
